5.1  Modulation             
In telecommunication, the information or â€˜messageâ€™ signal (such as voice or 
music) usually has a low frequency, called the baseband signal . However, this 
low-frequency signal is unsuitable for direct long-distance transmission using a 
practical antenna. To overcome this, we use a process called Modulation. 
Modulation is defined as the process of varying a parameter (amplitude, 
frequency, or phase)  of a high -frequency carrier signal in accordance with the 
instantaneous value of the low-frequency information signal. 
In simple words, modulation is the technique of â€˜superimposing information on 
a high-frequency carrier waveâ€™ so that it can be transmitted over long distances.

5.1.1 Key Signal Definitions 
â€¢ Modulating Signal (Message Signal):  This is the baseband signal that 
contains the actual information to be transmitted (e.g., audio from a 
microphone). It has low frequency and low energy. 
â€¢ Carrier Signal: This is a high-frequency sinusoidal wave produced by an 
oscillator. It acts as a "carrier" that transports the message through the 
medium. It contains no information of its own. 
â€¢ Modulated Signal:  The resulting wave after the modulation process, 
which contains the characteristics of both the message and the carrier.

Modulation is essential in modern communication systems for several technical 
reasons:

Under-Modulation ( Î¼ < 1):  When the modulation index is less than 1, the 
condition is called under -modulation. In this case, the modulating signal 
amplitude is less than the carrier amplitude (Am < Ac). The AM envelope does not 
reach zero, and the minimum amplitude A min is positive. Under -modulation 
results in inefficient use of transmitter power because a significant portion of 
power remains in the carrier, which carries no information. However, the signal 
is free from distortion. 
Critical Modulation (Î¼ = 1 or 100% Modulation): When the modulation index 
equals 1, it is called critical modulation or 100% modulation. In this case, the 
amplitude of the modulating signal equals the carrier amplitude (A m = Ac). The 
AM envelope just touches zero at the minimum point (A min = 0), and reaches 
twice the carrier amplitude at the maximum (A max = 2A c). This represents the 
ideal condition for AM transmission, as it provides maximum power efficiency

5.4  Phase Modulation (PM)         
Phase Modulation (PM) is a modulation technique in which the phase of the 
carrier signal is varied in accordance with the instantaneous value of the 
modulating signal, while the amplitude and frequency of the carrier remain 
constant. In PM, information is conveyed through variations in the phase angle 
of the carrier wave. 
The basic principle of phase modulation is that when a modulating signal is 
applied, the phase of the carrier signal changes instantaneously according to the 
amplitude of the modulating signal. A positive modulating signal causes a phase 
advance, while a negative modulating signal causes a phase delay relative to the 
unmodulated carrier.

5.4.3 Relationship Between FM and PM 
Phase modulation and frequency modulation are closely related, as both fall 
under the category of angle modulation. In fact, phase modulation can be 
considered as a special case of frequency modulation, and vice versa. The key 
relationship is that phase is  the integral of frequency, and frequency is the 
derivative of phase with respect to time. 
When a signal is phase modulated, the instantaneous frequency also varies, 
making it appear similar to FM. Similarly, when a signal is frequency modulated, 
the phase also changes. The fundamental difference is: 
â€¢ In FM, the instantaneous frequency deviation is directly proportional to 
the amplitude of the modulating signal. 
â€¢ In PM, the phase deviation is directly proportional to the amplitude of the 
modulating signal, which means the instantaneous frequency deviation is 
proportional to the derivative of the modulating signal.

5.5  Introduction to Multiplexing         
In a telecommunication system, several users need to transmit information 
simultaneously over a common communication medium â€” such as a coaxial 
cable, optical fiber, microwave link, or wireless channel. Providing a separate 
physical channel for each user would be both costly and impractical. 
Multiplexing is the technique that solves this problem by allowing multiple 
independent signals to share a single transmission medium efficiently.

Multiplexing is a technique by which multiple independent signals are combined 
into one composite signal, transmitted over a shared communication channel, 
and then separated back into the original individual signals at the receiving end. 
5.5.2 Need for Multiplexing 
Multiplexing is essential in modern communication for the following reasons: 
â€¢ Efficient Bandwidth Utilisation: Most communication media possess a 
much higher bandwidth than a single user requires. Multiplexing allows 
this excess bandwidth to be shared among several users, ensuring no 
capacity is wasted. 
â€¢ Cost Reduction:  Installing separate cables or links for every user is 
expensive. A single multiplexed channel can serve many users, drastically 
reducing infrastructure and maintenance costs.

Frequency Division Multiplexing (FDM) is an analog multiplexing technique in 
which the total available bandwidth of a communication channel is divided into 
several non-overlapping frequency sub-bands. Each input signal is assigned one 
sub-band and all sign als are transmitted simultaneously, each occupying a 
different frequency range. Separation of signals is therefore achieved in the 
frequency domain.
